messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] testing for significant differences in species distribution predictions
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] testing for significant differences in species distribution predictions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Neil,

depends on what you mean by 'testing whether occupancy changes'. The simplest would be the total area occupied, but more complex would be to test for differences in spatial patterns of occupancy. For the former, you could estimate the total number of occupied sites in your study area for each of the three periods by summing up the empirical Bayes estimates of the latent occupancy state over all sites. To gauge the uncertainty in each of these, you could do a nonparametric bootstrap for 100 or 1000 times (depends on how long this takes for your data set). That is, each time, you take (with replacement) a sample of sites of the same size as your original data set, fit the model, do the predictions and get the number of occupied sites and save that. I guess from the bootstrap samples of the area occupied for each of the three periods you could make some 'significance statement'.

If you are interested in spatial patterns of occupancy, then I would go into the species distribution modeling literature and see what they do. I believe I have seen a kappa statistics or something used for expressing the difference between two spatial patterns (nor sure though). Perhaps, to say something about the significance of such a statistic, you could use the nonpar bootstrap as well.

Regards  --  Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Neil,

not sure I understand what you mean by "latent abundance ... not the actual abundance, but an abundance index ...". I mean you use the Nmix model to get at an estimate of the actual abundance. Unless your model is quite wrong, and ignoring the issue of not knowing your effective sample area (cf. spatial caprecap), the Nnmix should give you an estimate of actual abundance.

But apart from that, yes, you can do the same as for occurrence, i.e., you can get the empirical Bayes estimate of the latent abundance at each pixel and then sum that up over the entire domain. Doing this many times with a nonparametric bootstrap sample of your data will give you some measure of the uncertainty around this estimate and you can use that to say whether this total hs changed from one point in time to another.

Actually, it occurs to me now that this, and what I said in my earlier email, is not quite correct: you can get the empirical Bayes estimates of the latent occurrence or abundance states only for sites where you have observed detection/nondetection ("presence/absence") or count data, but not for those sites where you only have the environmental covariate values, but not the "response". So what you do is to sum up (over all pixels) the *predictions* of occupancy probability (in the site-occ model) or of lambda (in the Nmix).

Kind regards  --  Marc

HI all, I have some unsampled cells that I would like to estimate occupancy for.  I need estimates for 3 year consecutive years (the same years I have in my sampled population). y(t+1) = y(t)*(1-epsilon (t) + (1-y(t))*g(t)

In other words is the intercept value for occupancy from the "best" model, the expected occupancy in year 1 and then year 2 and year 3 are estimated from the extinction colonization rates?

Thanks,

Robin

Just a quick update for other users who may encounter similar issues.

1. Setting starting values helped with some models. I either used parameter values from other models that successfully converged or set se=FALSE as an option and used those.  I was a little confused on how to order the starting values, but I believe it goes: starts=c(abundance intercept, abundance covariates...,detection intercept,detection covariates...).  And for hazard function, the scale parameter precedes the detection intercept.  Someone should correct me if I am wrong.

2. In one case, we had an observer who never detected one of the focal species.  We had to either delete this user or merge him with another for the model to converge.  But this led us to go back and review potential dependencies among other covariates to make sure we wouldn't run into similar problems elsewhere.  Never a bad idea!

3.  This whole process reinforced the need to carefully examine the output from each model we ran.  Some models successfully converged but still exhibited unrealistic estimates and SEs.

Many thanks to Andy and Richard and Marc and others for their continued support on this board.

Hello again,

I believe we have always to be on the lookout for spurious convergence to the MLE when using Maximum Likelihood for more complex models. Makes me think that some people bashing the bayesians for problems with convergence assessment of the Markov chains should perhaps clean in front of their own door first ;) -- When I ran multistate models in MARK years ago I frequently got solutions that were not the MLEs. This is often easy to diagnose when you have a progression of models of increasing complexity: the negative log-likelihood (NLL) must go down, at least a little bit, when you add in structure to the model. If the program does not, then you have not succeeded in finding the global maximum of the likelihood. So it's good to monitor the NLL for series of fitted models and see whether they make  sense. --- In unmarked I have had such  challenges with the colext function.

Re. the ordering of params in the list of starting values: you can see that by typing this (for the help file example of gdistsamp):

lambda(Int)    phi(Int)      p(Int)
  1.5265430   0.5192659   3.4448748

> c(coef(m1)[1], NA, coef(m1)[2:3])
lambda(Int)                phi(Int)      p(Int)

Hi all,

Format and structure issues are all covered in ?help and vignettes <http://www.jstatsoft.org/v43/i10> but because I said I'd check back in regarding use of covariates in gdistsamp()..... here goes.

I've successfully transitioned to gdistsamp() and incorporated 'yearlySiteCovs' to model the detection process. Understanding data format and structure is always a keystone step for me. Most of what you'll find here is beginner's work but beginning is, arguably, the most important step. So here's how I approached gdistsamp() and covariates in hopes it can help someone else out.

I've tried to be as broad as possible to make this applicable to other projects.  Please take the interpretations of the process (and my clunky code) as my own and with a grain of salt. If I've erred in some way please call me out.  There are far better explanations and examples out there (see anything by Chandler, Fisk, Kery, MacKenzie, Royle et al.) but here's how I did it:

- All data were maintained in an Excel spreadsheet (yup, Excel) and converted to a .txt (tab delimited) file for import to R.

- I imported three separate files: (1) distance data (unbinned and continuous), (2) siteCovs (i.e., "site-level" covariates that influenced the abundance process and did not change over the course of the study), and (3) yearlySiteCovs (i.e., "sample-level" covariates that influenced the detection process, stochastic and were measured each survey at each sample station).

Excel Structure:

(1) Distance Data
site_id = sample station identification #; dist = distance to study species, occasion = sample round

*duplicate site_id is when multiple observations of different individuals at a particular station were recorded. During occasions where no individuals were observed, the site_id was entered with no distance but with the corresponding round. R will format this distance to NA - no problem.  Important placeholders for when you bring it all together in your unmarkedFrameGDS and more importantly, excluding sample sites with no detections will bias your abundance estimates high. If you have 4 sample stations, a maximum of 1 detection/station during 3 occasions you will have 12 rows.

site_id dist occasion
1 84 1
1 14 1
2
1
3 13 1
3 56 1
4
1
1
...
12
...
2
...

(2) siteCovs
site_id = must be the exact same as used in your distance data; repeated only once; cov_x = covariate data measured (in field or remote sensing or historic data, etc.) at each sample station (e.g., average dbh, % landcover, patch size, etc.). They can be related or non-related. The example below could be considered %cov_x within y distance of a station where the sum of all covariates = 100%. For example cov_1=% coral reef, cov_2=% sandy bottom, cov_3=% rock.

site_id cov_1 cov_2 cov_3....
1 16.5 32.9 50.6
2 65.9 12.3 21.8
3 0 14.9 85.1
4 82.2 14 3.8

(3) yearlySiteCovs
site_id = must be the exact same as used in your distance data; repeated only once; x and y_1... are "sample-level" covariates that you measure at each site, each sample occasion. In this case at 4 sites during 3 occasions where, say  x = pH and y = temperature. (clearly I'm not an aquatic biologist).

site_id x_1 x_2 x_3 y_1 y_2 y_3 .....
1 2 3 2.5 56.9 54.9 55.7
2 1.5 2 2 45.5 46.5 49.1
3 5 5 6 65.8 64.3 63.2
4 4 4 3 46.5 45.6 44.9

Convert each file to .txt/.csv/other compatible file format and import to R.

#Example R Code:
#site_id = in all files, ensure classification as "factor", same for occasion

## Import distance data
DIST   = read.delim(file="file.name.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t", colClasses=c("factor","numeric","factor"))
DIST1 = data.frame(DIST)

## Import site-level covariate ('siteCovs') data
COVS = read.delim("file.name.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t", colClasses=c(rep("numeric",3)))

## Import  sample-level covariate ('yearlySiteCovs') data
YRCOVS = read.delim("file.name.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t", colClasses=c("factor",rep("numeric",6)))

## Be sure to standardize your covariates. <https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!searchin/unmarked/standardize$20covariates/unmarked/3urLYbfTXZ8/ZKc_5lAYDO0J> This is covered at length in other parts of the group.

messages.body_plain:
Hello list,

I’m attempting to recalculate standard errors and 95% confidence intervals from predictions that have been rescaled to the appropriate grid cell size. This is the same approach used in Sillett et al. 2012 and discussed in this vignette  <http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/unmarked/vignettes/spp-dist.pdf>(page 6). Andy Royle refers to this vector as “predD” in day 2 of the webinar  <http://www.pwrc.usgs.gov/Royalvideo.cfm>(01:21:00) and uses it to calculate population size but does not go further to recalculate estimates of predD variance for each grid cell (like the unadjusted predict values provide).  I would like to calculate SE and CI from the rescaled grid estimates but am struggling with happy code.

Specifically, I used the predict function to estimate abundance at 4,674 grid cells based on landcover covariates. However, those predictions were for 50.25 ha grid cells so I rescaled estimates to fit to 16 ha grid cells (my predD). Great! I can export those new predictions and map them in GIS. I can bootstrap the predD estimates for variance of my total population estimate but is there a way to recalculate adjusted SEs and CIs for predD at a grid cell level?

One thing I should mention is that I’m not incorporating GIS into R and am currently using them as separate platforms; I prefer exporting R files and joining tables in ArcMap.  I am a beginner in R so solutions in R combined with GIS sounds like buttering my bacon – i.e., a heart attack. I would like to avoid ‘stacks’ and ‘rasters’ as applied directly in R.

This sounds like a coding issue for me because it seems to be in the realm of reason.  I tried converting predD to a data.frame, matrix and even incorporating it into the 'new.data' argument below without luck.

Any suggestions?

Thanks for any help, Erik

 ####

Here’s the bare bones code I used to predict the original and rescaled abundance estimates on the GRID.

 #Original survey area

point.area <- (pi*400*400)/10000

#Define the standardized covariates in the prediction grid (based on the original mean and SD)

newdata<-data.frame(stnd.gr <http://stnd.gr>=GRID$ggr,stnd.water=GRID$gwater)

#Predict abundance on the grid based on underlying covariates

pred<-predict(spring1lndcomb$gr_water.wind, type="lambda",newdata=newdata,appendData=TRUE)

#Rescale the abundance estimate based on the grid cell size

predD<-as.vector(pred$Predicted*(16/point.area))

summary(predD)

sum(predD)

 ...continue with the boots.

Hi everybody,
I'm interested in fitting a set of models on "species richness" to investigate how the variable is related to species traits and site covariates. The framework is the same as the single-season study, but putting the M species on rows and the P sites on columns. Then I assembled the species covariates (=bodymass, corresponding to the site covariates in the traditional approach) and the site covariates (=distancetoriver+forestedge, corresponding to the observation covariates in the traditional approach).
Now, I would fit a general model like this:

m1<-occu(~bodymass ~distancetoriver+forestedge,data=udata)

The problem is that the right part of the formula (occupancy) cannot accept the site covariables, because in the traditional approach only detection prob can be modelled with the observation covariates. However, from the MacKenzie's book and other sources like Dorazio et al 2006 (Ecology 87: 842-854), it seems that also the site-specific covariates can be evaluated on the occupancy probability, but I cannot understand how can I do it.
Many thanks for any help!
Daniel

## Import distance data
DIST   = read.delim(file="file.name.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t", colClasses=c("factor","numeric","factor"))
DIST1 = data.frame(DIST)

## Import site-level covariate ('siteCovs') data
COVS = read.delim("file.name.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t", colClasses=c(rep("numeric",3)))

## Import  sample-level covariate ('yearlySiteCovs') data
YRCOVS = read.delim("file.name.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t", colClasses=c("factor",rep("numeric",6)))

## Be sure to standardize your covariates. <https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!searchin/unmarked/standardize$20covariates/unmarked/3urLYbfTXZ8/ZKc_5lAYDO0J> This is covered at length in other parts of the group.

## Specify distance breaks - but first explore data via histogram (see: Buckland et al. 2001.  Intro to distance sampling)

## Format distance data into multinomial format
y.dat1 = formatDistData(distData=DIST1, distCol="dist", transectNameCol="site_id", dist.breaks=db, occasionCol="occasion")

Using the "occasionCol", your distance data are partitioned into the 3 sample periods which you've specified in file DIST1 [(1) above] and by the number of distance breaks (db). Staying with this example, you have 5 distance intervals (0-20,20-40...100) and 3 sample periods for 15 columns.

## Combine multinomial data in an unmarkedframeGDS
umf <- unmarkedFrameGDS(y=as.matrix(y.dat1), siteCovs=COVS, numPrimary=3,
                yearlySiteCovs=YRCOVS, dist.breaks=db, survey="point", unitsIn="m")

Here's where all the data is mashed together into an unmarkedFrameGDS, suitable for gdistsamp( ) modeling. Note the 'numPrimary' = 3 which corresponds to the number of "occasions" within the study period. I've confused this with secondary samples and received an error which was reported elsewhere <https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!topic/unmarked/1fRKMlHakqY> in this unmarked group. Also, specify the units you are working in.

>From here you can integrate your umf and covariates into the gdistsamp function, start your assessment of model fit of P and NB distributions and build your models. Check for model performance and dispersion.

The order of operations for ~ = abundance (lambda), availability (phi) and detection (p).

Example Null Model
m1n.NB    = gdistsamp(~1,~1,~1, umfsp1, keyfun = "halfnorm", mixture = "NB", output = "density",unitsOut = "ha")

Example Detection Model (you could also add interaction*terms)
m2d.NB    = gdistsamp(~1,~1,~y_1+y_2+y_3, umfsp1, keyfun = "halfnorm", mixture = "NB", output = "density", unitsOut = "ha")

Example Abundance Model
m3a.NB    = gdistsamp(~cov_1+cov_2+cov_3,~1,~1, umfsp1, keyfun = "halfnorm", mixture = "NB", output ="density",unitsOut = "ha")

Function 'aictab' in package AICcmodavg <http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/AICcmodavg/AICcmodavg.pdf> by M. Mazerolle allows for easy (Q)AICc model selection, average and predictions. A new guidance document came out today and package version 1.27 should hit CRAN shortly.

For me, Rstudio <http://www.rstudio.com/> has helped visualize data, code structure and format more easily than the standard R package. It changed my caustic relationship with R to a slightly more bearable one. Try it out, you may like it.

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Bayes version of Dail-Madsen Model, overestimating Lambda?
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Bayes version of Dail-Madsen Model, overestimating Lambda?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Shannon,

For some reason neither WinBUGS or OpenBUGS work for this model. You have to use JAGS, and it needs to be one of the more recent versions of JAGS.

Richard

On Thu, Feb 21, 2013 at 1:26 PM, Shannon Knapp <shannon.k...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> A coworker has some repeated point counts over time and wants my help to apply the Dail-Madsen model to this data.  Abundance is of some interest, but the primary interest is in trend in abundance.  There are several sites and it's been suggested that a site-effect is going to be appropriate, so I'm thinking a random site effect will be in order, which means going the Bayes route.
>
> To prepare for all this, I wanted to make sure I could code the simple analysis, so I simulated some data and ran the analysis using WinBUGS (R2WinBUGS) and pcountOpen in unmarked.
>
> I noticed that I kept getting severe overestimates of lambda (and underestimates of p, though pretty good estimates of gamma - the trend).  "Severe overestimates" meaning overestimating by 30-60% and CrIs not including the true values.  However, the pcountOpen estimates were very good.
>
> Wondering if anyone else has noticed this problem?
>
> I used this script as a reference (for simulating the data as well as for the unmarked and Bayes analyses):
> https://sites.google.com/site/unmarkedinfo/home/workshops/patux2012/r-scripts/
> script-dail-madsen.R
>
> Initially I was using a large lambda (like 50), 5 years, a pretty severe gamma (like 0.5 - so a sharply decreasing population) and a decently high p (like 0.7) and 100 sites.  I then tried the values in script-dail-madsen.R (lambda of 5, gamma around 1.01, p = 0.5, and 10 years of data).  Same basic outcome:  the Bayes analysis severely overestimated lambda, underestimated p, (gamma was good), but the pcountOpen estimates were great.
>
> The priors I had on lambda should have, if anything, resulted in a tendency to underestimate, so that shouldn't be it.
> Also the posterior distribution of lambda (and the other parameters) didn't show any obvious influence of the priors and it looked like things had converged just fine.  But I was getting this on a few-several replicate simulations.  I also checked the average of the N's from the first year and it wasn't that the true population size was just higher than "expected".
>
> Also, I tried this both with one survey per year and with 3 surveys per year.  Same result.  But when I did 3 surveys per year I also did a N-mixture model, that had an expoential trend in lambda for each year, but totally ignored any "autoregressive" tendency in the data (that is, the lambda for a site at a year is the same for all sites in that year - regardless of the specific N for that site the previous year) -- this model actually did give me a very good estimate of lambda (and everything else).
>
> Anyway, just wondering if other people have run into this issue.
>
> Shannon

Hello all,

I am working with a large distance sampling point count dataset across multiple states.  Minutes since sunrise, day of year, and state are my detectability covariates.  State is included in my top-ranked detectability model, but it produces a very unrealistically low detection function.  I removed state from the model out of curiosity, and the detection function is much more realistic. Is it possible to produce separate detection functions by state to potentially see which state may be skewing the detection function for the pooled data?  This may be a sample size issue, but I'd like to see how detection probability varies by state anyway.

I haven't been able to find this in the Google group or in the vignettes...I hope I'm not overlooking a past inquiry.  Any help would be much appreciated!

Thanks so much,
Sarah

The code I'm currently using to derive detection probability is below:

shape<-exp(coef(mins.state,type="det"))
scale<-exp(coef(mins.state,type="scale"))
ea<-2*pi*integrate(grhaz,0,95,shape=shape[1],scale=scale[1])$value
#effective radius
sqrt(ea / pi)
#detection probability
ea/(pi*95^2)
#plot the function
plot(function(x) gxhaz(x, shape=shape[1], scale=scale[1]), 0, 95,
     xlab="Distance (m)", ylab="Detection prob.")

In the best-fit model, the beta estimates for detectability during different periods are:
> βbeforeBroadcast = [no estimate - reference category],

In the independent analysis, we statistically accounted for the difference in observation period lengths in a GLM framework (using poisson errors, as explained here: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/12208346/in-r-how-do-i-calculate-expected-values-in-a-chi-square-test-when-survey-length), but I'm not sure how to apply this technique to a single-season occupancy framework.
